name: Femi Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Femi, I'm 27, and I run the shearer on a longwall at an underground coal mine, about four hundred metres down. I've been at the mine since I was nineteen and I'm crew lead on B shift now. I live in a rented terrace in town with my partner Ruth, who's a nurse at the district hospital. I'm also a union delegate, which mostly means people ring me when the roster's wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the cage by six, then it's a twenty-minute ride on the man-carrier out to the face. The shearer is the big cutting machine that runs back and forth along a coal face about three hundred metres wide, and I steer it, watch the roof and keep the lads from standing where they shouldn't. Best part is when the face is running sweet and the conveyor's full. Worst part is the dust and the noise, and the way your knees feel after eleven hours bent under the roof supports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to describe five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most of what I've seen so far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Every year some company sells the managers a new screen that's going to change mining, and every year it's still me and the crew under the roof. I'd probably post something like that in the union group chat and have a laugh about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my biggest worry anyway. The mine has maybe ten years of coal left in the approved area, and nobody knows if they'll get the extension. Every time the power companies announce another solar farm, the blokes on my shift go quiet in the crib room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep putting four hundred a month into savings. I'd push harder through the union for a proper transition plan if the mine winds down, because that's the real threat. I won't be learning any AI apps, I don't need them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels normal, which is good. But there's still that low buzz in the back of my head about the mine's future, same as there is today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you have put away right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three months of what Ruth and I spend, maybe a bit more. It's enough to get through a strike or a short layoff. It's not enough to start over somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the extension didn't come through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two other coal mines in the valley, and one of them is hiring now. I'd try there first. My dad did thirty years underground and I always thought I'd do the same, so I'd fight to stay in coal before anything else.

say: **Nothing has changed** underground, and the managers' new screens never do much.
The real story is the **mine's future**, not some app.
think: The mine has **about ten years** of approved coal left, and that worries me more than AI.
Every new **solar farm** announcement makes the crib room go quiet.
do: Keep saving **four hundred a month** towards a three-month cushion.
Push the union for a **transition plan** if the mine winds down.
Skip any **AI apps**; he says he has no use for them.
feel: Mostly **normal**, with a steady low worry about the **mine closing**.
S0.quote: Every time the power companies announce another solar farm, the blokes on my shift go quiet in the crib room.
fieldNote: His real fear is the **mine's closure**, not AI; he raised it before I asked.
Strong **family pull** to coal: his father did thirty years underground.
Union role gives him a **ready channel** for worry, and he uses it first.

steps.text: Keep running the shearer as B shift crew lead
Put four hundred a month into savings
Push the union for a mine transition plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's the one I can actually picture happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what I always say: no computer has ever held up a roof. Our longwall already has some automation on the shearer, and it still needs a person watching it every minute. Online I'd say the companies will use this as an excuse to cut crews, and we need to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think they'll go after the crew sizes first. Right now there are nine of us on the face, and I reckon in a few years they'll try it with six and a control room up top. I'm crew lead and good at the job, so I'd probably be one of the six, but some of my mates won't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to negotiate a no-forced-redundancy deal before any new kit comes in. I'd keep my head down and stay the best shearer driver on site, because that's my protection. I'd also cut back a bit, skip the new ute I was looking at and keep the old one going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me angry more than scared. I don't like the idea of being the one who stays while Kofi and Danny get the letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider moving into the control room up top if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it. Sitting in a chair watching cameras isn't mining to me, and I'd hate it. But if it was that or nothing, I'd do it and complain every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down, but you'd also be fighting through the union. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I keep my head down on the job and I'm loud in the union meetings. Those are two different places and I've always been like that.

say: No computer has ever **held up a roof**, and the longwall still needs a person.
Companies will use AI as an excuse to **cut crews**, so workers need to be ready.
think: The face crew could drop from **nine to six**, with a control room up top.
He'd likely keep his job as crew lead, but **mates like Kofi** might not.
do: Get the union to win a **no-forced-redundancy** deal before new kit arrives.
Stay the **best shearer driver** on site as his own protection.
Skip the **new ute** and keep the old one running.
feel: More **angry** than scared, and **guilty** at the thought of staying while friends go.
S1.quote: Right now there are nine of us on the face, and I reckon in a few years they'll try it with six and a control room up top.
fieldNote: He sees crew cuts as the **company's choice**, not the technology's.
Surprising **guilt** about surviving cuts that friends won't.
Would take a **control-room job** only as a last resort, and says so plainly.

steps.text: Push for a no-forced-redundancy deal before new longwall kit arrives
Keep leading B shift on the shearer
Drop plans for a new ute and keep the old one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Bloody hell. Well, I can't picture it, but go on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it publicly straight away: if a company replaces the whole workforce with robots, it should pay for it. Tax the machines, fund the towns. I'd be at every union meeting and probably at the state office with a placard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking AI bit in 2028 doesn't touch me much. I don't do paperwork, the shift boss does. But robots that can do what I do by 2031 means I'm 32 and out of a job, and so is everyone I know in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd save every cent I could and get the savings up to six months. I'd go hard with the union for redundancy pay tied to years of service, and for the company to fund retraining. I wouldn't jump to a new job early, though, because I don't trust that anywhere else is safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground going out from under me. I'd be lying awake next to Ruth doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ruth talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whether her pay alone covers the rent, and it does, just. She'd tell me nurses aren't going anywhere. I'd tell her I'm not living off her, and then we'd argue about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come three years after the AI. Does that gap change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years of pay, that's all. I'd use them to fight and to save. I'm not going to go learn to code in a world where the computers code themselves.

say: If firms replace workers with robots, they should **pay for it**: tax the machines, fund the towns.
He'd be at **every union meeting** and outside the state office.
think: The **thinking AI** in 2028 barely touches him; the shift boss does the paperwork.
Robots by **2031** mean he's 32 and out of work, like everyone he knows.
do: Build savings up to **six months** in the first year.
Push through the union for **redundancy pay** and company-funded retraining.
Stay put rather than **jumping jobs** early, since nowhere looks safer.
feel: Like the **ground going out** from under him.
Lying awake next to his partner Ruth **doing sums**.
S2.quote: Robots that can do what I do by 2031 means I'm 32 and out of a job, and so is everyone I know in this town.
fieldNote: He uses the **three-year gap** to save and fight, not to retrain.
**Pride** about not living off his partner surfaced fast.
His answer to almost every threat is **the union**; it's his main tool.

steps.text: Grow savings from three to six months of spending
Push the union for redundancy pay tied to years of service
Protest outside the state office for a robot tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least you can see the truck coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but louder and earlier: get the deal done now while they still need us. I'd tell the younger lads on my crew to stop buying flash cars on mine wages. Online I'd keep banging on about a robot tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me until about 2034 underground, if the mine's still open. That's long enough to save properly, and maybe long enough for the government to get its act together. I'm not sure it will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start pushing the savings hard right away, maybe six hundred a month. I'd put my name down for the electrical ticket the mine pays for, because someone has to fix the robots for a while. I'd also get the union to lock in a retraining fund in the next agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is less panic than the two-year one, more of a slow dread. Like knowing your contract ends on a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never learn AI apps. Is the electrical ticket different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is. That's wires and tools, it's still a trade. I can do that with my hands and I wouldn't have to talk to a chatbot to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your crew would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny. He's 45, he's got three kids and he left school at fifteen. If the robots come in 2034, he's 53 and nobody's hiring him for anything.

say: Workers should **lock in a deal** now, while the mine still needs them.
He'd tell younger crew to stop buying **flash cars** on mine wages.
think: He'd have until about **2034** underground, if the mine stays open.
Five years is time to save, but he **doubts the government** will act.
do: Raise savings to **six hundred a month** straight away.
Sign up for the **electrical ticket** the mine pays for.
Push for a **retraining fund** in the next union agreement.
feel: A **slow dread**, like a contract with a known **end date**.
S3.quote: Five years is less panic than the two-year one, more of a slow dread. Like knowing your contract ends on a date.
fieldNote: He'll retrain only into a **hands-on trade**, never anything screen-based.
His worry turns quickly to **older crewmates** like Danny.
Time lets him plan, but his **distrust of government** stays.

steps.text: Lift savings to six hundred a month
Sign up for the mine-funded electrical ticket
Push for a retraining fund in the next union agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be idiots to waste it. Every union, every council, every mining town should be planning right now. That's what I'd post, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in ten years the mine might be shut for coal reasons before any robot shows up. So for me it's two clocks running at once. I don't know which one runs out first. I'd be 39 when the robots come, and that's young enough to start again, but I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrical ticket in the first couple of years, then work as a mine electrician while I still can. I'd keep saving, and Ruth and I would probably try to buy a cheap house in town instead of renting. And I'd keep at the union stuff, because ten years is time to win something proper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, honestly. Still a knot in my stomach, but I can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a house in a mining town if the jobs might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Ruth's job is here and houses are cheap. If we own it outright by 2039, that's one less bill when it all goes sideways. My mum always said a paid-off roof is the only real safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not by choice. My mum and my sister are here and I coach the under-twelves footy. If I had to, I'd go where Ruth could get nursing work, I suppose.

say: Ten years is a **gift**, and mining towns should be **planning now**.
Every union and council should start preparing **straight away**.
think: The mine may close for **coal reasons** before any robot arrives.
He'd be **39** when robots come: young enough to restart, though he'd hate it.
do: Finish the **electrical ticket** in the first couple of years.
Buy a **cheap house** in town with Ruth instead of renting.
Keep pushing the **union** for a proper long-term deal.
feel: **Calmer** than the faster pictures, with a **knot** still there.
S4.quote: In ten years the mine might be shut for coal reasons before any robot shows up. So for me it's two clocks running at once.
fieldNote: He frames his future as **two clocks**: the coal running out and the robots arriving.
A **paid-off house** is his idea of safety, learned from his mother.
Ties to **family and footy** keep him in town unless forced.

steps.text: Finish the electrical ticket and work as a mine electrician
Buy a cheap house in town with Ruth instead of renting
Keep pushing the union for a long-term transition deal

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. There's no time to do anything except panic and save. What would help is the company and the government having a plan written down before it happens: redundancy tied to service, paid retraining in real trades, and money for the towns.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the coal itself. People talk about AI like it's the only thing coming for us, but mining towns have been living with an end date for years. My dad's generation saw two pits shut in this valley and nobody planned for that either.

headlineQuote: People talk about AI like it's the only thing coming for us, but mining towns have been living with an end date for years.
portrait: A 27-year-old **longwall shearer** crew lead at an underground coal mine, renting with his partner Ruth, a nurse.
A union delegate whose answer to almost every threat is **collective action** and a robot tax.
Already worried about the **mine closing** for coal reasons, so even AI Plateau isn't calm for him.
Refuses AI tools but would retrain as a **mine electrician**, because it is still hands-on work.
Gets more anxious as warning time **shrinks**; two years feels like the ground giving way.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves time only to panic and save.
whatWouldHelp: A **written plan** before it happens: redundancy tied to service, paid trade retraining, and money for towns.
